q: What is primarily concerned with judging the true value of statements and seeking errors?
n: Critical thinking judges the truth of statements and looks for errors. Source: Paul & Elder, Critical Thinking (2006).

q: What type of forms consist of a number of secondary forms clustered about a dominant parent forms?
n: Centralized forms are secondary forms clustered around a dominant central parent form. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order, Ch. 2 (Additive Forms).

q: Additive forms consisting of a number of secondary forms clustered around a center
n: Centralized forms are secondary forms clustered around a dominant central form. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 2 (Additive Forms).

q: The balanced arrangement of similar elements such that the composition can be divided into similar halves by passing a plane at any angle along a central axis.
n: Radial symmetry: any plane through the central axis divides the composition into similar halves. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7 (Symmetry).

q: A type of balance in design principle wherein elements are arranged equally around a central point.
n: Radial balance arranges elements equally around a central point. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: The principle that reflects the degree of importance of forms and spaces as well as the functional and symbolic roles they play
n: Hierarchy expresses the relative importance and functional or symbolic roles of forms and spaces. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7 (Hierarchy).

q: A design principle wherein an architectural element appears more important in comparison to other elements in a design
n: Hierarchy makes one element appear more important than the others. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: A museum seeks to integrate a traditional architectural art form that permanently depicts historical events, rules, and cultural narrative through sculpted imagery on wall and facade surfaces. Which art form is most appropriate?
o: Transition from Dark Space to Light Space
n: Bas-relief permanently records history and culture in sculpted wall and facade surfaces. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which artistic elements are mast directly used to evoke emotional responses and influence the psychological experience of architectural spaces?
n: Color and texture are the artistic elements that most directly shape emotional response to a space. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.); Mahnke, Color, Environment, and Human Response.

q: When selecting a traditional decorative element primarily to enhance the visual beauty and artistic character of an interior space, which design objective is being emphasized?
n: Choosing decoration mainly for visual beauty serves aesthetics. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.).

q: Which traditional architectural art form is primarily employed to enhance visual appeal through color, light, and ornamental composition?
n: Stained glass enhances interiors through color, light and ornamental composition. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which traditional architectural art form contributes not only to visual appeal but also to environmental performance through shading, privacy, and ventilation?
n: Wood lattice (calado) is decorative and also shades, gives privacy and lets air through. Source: Lico, Arkitekturang Filipino; Lechner, Heating, Cooling, Lighting.

q: When integrating traditional art forms into a building envelope while improving shading and airflow, which treatment is most appropriate for the facade?
n: Wood lattice on the facade adds traditional craft while improving shade and airflow. Source: Lico, Arkitekturang Filipino.

q: Which conternporary art form best represents the integration of digital technology and architecture for dynamic visual expression?
n: LED media walls combine digital technology and architecture for changing visual displays. Source: Haeusler, Media Facades (2009).

q: Which type of balance is achieved when visual elements are organized around a central point, radiating outward in all directions?
n: Radial balance organizes elements around a central point, radiating outward. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: In architectural composition, which type of balance is achieved when identical or similar elements are arranged equally on opposite sides of a central axis, creating a strong sense of order and stability?
n: Symmetrical balance places identical or similar elements equally on either side of a central axis. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: Which type of balance is achieved when identical or similar elements are arranged equally on opposite sides of a central axis, creating a strong sense of stability, order, and symmetry?
n: Formal (symmetrical) balance mirrors similar elements about a central axis. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: Among the different design principles of balance, which is more complex and difficult to achieve?
n: Asymmetrical balance is harder to achieve because unlike elements must be weighed against each other by judgment. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: In architectural design, which type of balance achieves visual equilibrium through the careful arrangement of dissimilar elements rather than mirrored symmetry?
n: Informal (asymmetrical) balance reaches equilibrium by carefully arranging dissimilar elements. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater achieves visual equilibrium without mirroring identical forms on either side of a central axis. Its composition is defined by projecting cantilevered terraces of different lengths, shifting masses, and an irregular relationship with the surrounding landscape. Which compositional principle is most evident?
n: Fallingwater balances unequal cantilevers and shifting masses, an asymmetrical composition. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.); Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.

q: The Taj Mahal in Agra, India is arranged around a dominant central axis. The mausoleum, gardens, reflecting pools, gateways, and minarets are positioned in a mirrored configuration so that one side closely reflects the other. Which principle of architectural composition is evident?
n: The Taj Mahal complex is mirrored about its central axis: symmetry. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.); UNESCO, Taj Mahal.

q: Viewed from the principal facade, St. Peter's Basilica presents a composition organized around a central axis, with matching architectural elements balanced on either side of the dome and entrance sequence. The overall design conveys order, stability, and formal equilibrium through mirrored organization. Which cormmpositional principle is most evident?
n: St. Peter's facade balances matching elements either side of the central axis: symmetry. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.).

q: Upon entering Hagia Sophia, a visitor is guided through a deliberate sequence of spaces leading toward the massive central dome. The architectural arrangement establishes a strong directional line that organizes movement, visual focus, and spatial progression from entrance to focal point. Which organizing principle is most evident?
n: Hagia Sophia's entrance sequence follows a strong line to the dome, which is an axis. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7 (Axis).

q: A visitor walking through the Salk Institute notices the repeated laboratory blocks, consistent spacing of openings, and the orderly progression of architectural elements along the plaza. This repetition creates a sense of movement and visual continuity throughout the composition. Which design principle is most evident?
n: The Salk Institute's repeated lab blocks and openings create rhythm. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7 (Rhythm).

q: The Palace of Versailles is organized so that the most important spaces, particularly those associated with the king, occupy dominant positions along the principal axis and are distinguished by greater size, richness, and ceremonial importance. Which design principle is most evident?
n: At Versailles the king's spaces lie on the main axis with greater size and richness: hierarchy. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: The Pantheon in Rome is organized around a central point, with its circular plan, dome, and interior spaces radiating outward from the center. Which organizational principle is most evident?
n: The Pantheon is organized around a central point with spaces radiating out, a centralized (radial) organization. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 4.

q: Although composed of multiple shell-like structures, the Sydney Opera House is perceived as a single coherent architectural composition because its forms, materials, geometry, and overall concept work together as one complete design. Which design principle is most evident?
n: The Sydney Opera House's shells read as one coherent composition: unity. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.).

q: In architectural composition, which type of balance is created when elements of different sizes, shapes, or visual weights are arranged to achieve equilibrium without relying on symmetry?
n: Informal (asymmetrical) balance arranges unequal elements in equilibrium without symmetry. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: An architect carefully adjusts the relationship between mass and void so that a new building responds harmoniously to the scale, open spaces, and built forms of its surroundings without visually dominating the site. Which design principle is being emphasized?
n: Contextual balance sets the mass–void relationship to suit the surrounding scale and open spaces. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.); Bentley et al., Responsive Environments.

q: An architect adjusts the proportion of mass and void so that forces are properly transferred to building elements, open spaces, and solid building forms can coexist while maintaining visual harmony, overall integrity and equilibrium te the system. Which type of balance is most critical in this situation?
n: When forces must travel properly through the elements while solids and voids coexist, structural balance is critical. Source: Salvadori & Heller, Structure in Architecture.

q: Which type of symmetry is achieved when opposing sides of a composition are not identical but are sufficiently similar in size, form, or visual weight to create a balanced appearance?
n: Approximate symmetry: the sides are not identical but are similar enough in size, form or weight to look balanced. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: Which design principle describes a state of visual equilibrium that conveys movement, energy, or tension while still maintaining overall stability within a composition?
n: Dynamic balance conveys movement, energy or tension while staying stable overall. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 7.

q: In a first-year design studio exercise inspired by Bauhaus foundation pedagogy, students were asked to generate spatial order using the most fundamental architectural element. The instructor emphasized that this element emerges from the movement of a point, establishes direction, and becomes the basis for alignment, rhythm, and organizational axes. Which architectural element is being described?
n: A line, a point in motion, sets direction and is the basis of alignment, rhythm and axes. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 1 (Primary Elements).

q: According to the principles of form and space, a line extended perpendicular to its length generates which architectural elerrent?
n: A line extended in a direction other than its own becomes a plane. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 1.

q: A student model demonstrates how a single element—created by the movement of a line—can define boundaries, surfaces, and fields of enclosure. This element has length and width but negligible thickness, and it becomes the generator of walls, floors, and ceilings. Which architectural element is being described?
n: A plane, a line in motion, has length and width but negligible thickness. It generates walls, floors and ceilings. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 1.

q: A plane extended in a direction other than its intrinsic direction generates which architectural element?
n: A plane extended in a direction other than its own becomes a volume. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 1.

q: In architectural design, space becomes perceptible and usable when it is defined by physical elements such as walls, floors, roofs, colurnns, or changes in level. The degree to which these elements establish boundaries determines the character of the space, ranging from fully enclosed interiors to partially bounded outdoor areas. What term best describes this process of defining space through architectural boundaries?
n: Defining space with walls, floors, roofs, columns or level changes is spatial enclosure. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 3.

q: In a spatial composition study, a student transforms a planar surface by extending it vertically, creating an entity with measurable length, width, and height. The instructor notes that this new condition is no longer a boundary but an enclosure, capable of containing space. Which architectural element is being described?
n: A plane extended to have length, width and depth becomes a volume, which can contain and enclose space. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 1.

q: A pavilion consists only of a floor plane, a roof canopy, and a series of columns. Although the space is clearly defined, it remains visually and physically continuous with the surrounding environment because some enclosing planes are absent. According to architectural theory, this type of spatial enclosure is best described as
n: A floor, a roof and columns define an open volume that stays continuous with its surroundings. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 3.

q: A room enclosed by walls, a floor, and a ceiling.creates a clearly bounded interior space with strong spatial definition and separation from adjacent areas. According to architectural theory, this type of spatial enclosure is best described as
n: A room bounded by walls, floor and ceiling is a closed volume. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 3.

q: In architectural composition; the area occupied by a form, mass, or object that command visual attention and defines the primary figure within a composition is known as
n: Positive space is the area occupied by the dominant figure or form. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 3 (figure–ground).

q: In architectural composition, the unoccupied area surrounding and between forms that helps define, emphasize, and give meaning to the primary figure is known as
n: Negative space is the unoccupied area around and between forms. It defines the figure. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 3.

q: A designer compares several architectural forms that share the same shape and material but differ in their physical dimensions. The comparison focuses on their measurable extents in length, width, and height rather than their proportions or relationship to surrounding objects. Which visual characteristic of form is being evaluated?
n: Comparing measurable length, width and height is evaluating size. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 2 (Properties of Form).

q: An architect studies how a building's surface appears and feels, considering whether it is smooth, rough, polished, coarse, reflective, or tactile. This characteristic influences the way light interacts with the surface and how users visually perceive the material. Which visual characteristic of form is being described?
n: How a surface looks and feels (smooth, rough, polished, reflective) is its texture. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 2.

q: A grand hotel lobby contains a circular lounge area defined by a ring of columns and a lowered ceiling plane. Although the lounge remains part of the larger lobby, it is perceived as a distinct zone within the larger volume. Which spatial relationship is being illustrated?
o: Spaces Linked by a Common Space
n: A ringed lounge inside a larger lobby is a space within a space. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 4 (Spatial Relationships).

q: A library and a reading lounge overlap physically, sharing a common area that belongs simultaneously to both functions. The overlapping zone serves as a transition between the two spaces while remaining part Gi each. Which spatia! relationship is being illustrated?
o: Spaces Linked by a Common Space
n: Overlapping spaces that share a zone are interlocking spaces. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 4.

q: In a residence, the dining room and living room are positioned directly beside one another, sharing a common wall but remaining separate and distinct spaces. Which spatial relationship is being illustrated?
o: Spaces Linked by a Common Space
n: Two rooms side by side sharing a wall are adjacent spaces. Source: Ching, Architecture: Form, Space and Order (4th ed.), Ch. 4.
